title: Turn 6: cast Edgar into the alpha-strike window, or keep casting Vampires?

board.you: Turn 6, precombat main, 30 life. Battlefield: Arcane Signet, Sanctum Seeker, Stromkirk Captain, four 1/1 black Vampire tokens (banked by eminence over turns 2-5), six lands producing all three colours, all untapped at the start of the phase. Edgar Markov is in the command zone — never cast. You just cast Knight of the Ebon Legion for {B}; once the eminence trigger resolves you will have exactly six mana left (five lands + Signet).
board.table: Player 2 (Esper draw-go; assume a bracket-4 sweeper deck holds a wrath when it passes with 4+ mana) is at 32 with four untapped lands and has cast almost nothing to the board all game. Player 3 (Gruul aggro) is at 12, tapped out, two creatures. Player 4 (Simic value engine) is at 38, ramping, two untapped lands, drawing extra cards every turn.

scenario.mana_available: 6 after the Knight resolves (five untapped lands + Arcane Signet)
stack: Eminence trigger (Edgar Markov, from the Knight of the Ebon Legion cast) — will create one 1/1 black Vampire token on resolution; that token enters this turn and cannot attack
scenario.extras: Attack math if Edgar is cast: attackers are Edgar (haste), Sanctum Seeker, Stromkirk Captain, and the four pre-existing tokens — seven attacking Vampires, the exact shape of verified stack 003 (here without Bloodletter, so seven Sanctum Seeker triggers = 7 life lost by EACH opponent at declare, before damage). Edgar's attack trigger puts a +1/+1 counter on every Vampire you control; Stromkirk Captain gives the team +1/+1 and first strike.
scenario.question: The eminence trigger is resolving and you must plan the turn: cast Edgar now and alpha-strike with the free-protection suite live, keep him zoned and double-spell into a bigger board (Bloodline Keeper + Vampire Socialite), or commit small and hold real-mana protection?

branches.choice: Cast Edgar now and alpha-strike with free Flawless Maneuver held
branches.line: Resolve the eminence token, then cast Edgar Markov for six — haste and first strike put him straight into the red zone. Swing with all seven eligible Vampires: seven Sanctum Seeker triggers drain every opponent 7 (Player 3 falls to 5 before damage), Edgar's trigger puts a counter on the whole team, and Stromkirk makes the tokens 3/3 first-strikers. Aim Edgar plus enough tokens at Player 3 to finish them through their two blockers. Flawless Maneuver costs {0} the whole way, because you now control a commander.
branches.signals: Casting Edgar is the loudest announcement this deck can make — the table has waited for it since turn 1. Good. The drains land at declare attackers, so even a fog or a mid-combat wrath arrives after each opponent has already lost 7. Player 2's four open lands are the question, and Flawless Maneuver is your literal answer to the destroy-based version of it.
branches.coalition_risk: High and accepted. You kill a player this turn, and the remaining game is 1-versus-2 with you as archenemy. You also removed the aggro deck that was racing you, and your engine survives the counterattack: eminence keeps producing whether Edgar lives or dies, and if he dies he returns to the zone with an 8-mana recast attached.
branches.coaching:
This board is the textbook pivot window — 'The window opens when your win attempt either can't be profitably answered — protection up, table tapped out, interaction counted and accounted for' — and you can count it. Player 3 is tapped out and dies. Player 4 holds two mana. Player 2's wrath is covered by a zero-mana Flawless Maneuver that Edgar's own resolution turned on.

That last point is the whole architecture of this deck: the free-protection suite is priced in Edgar. The turn you cast him is the turn you are safest, not the turn you are most exposed.

The honest costs. A counterspell on Edgar is the one clean beat — the drains still happen without him, and you attack with six next turn anyway. A -X/-X or exile sweeper goes under indestructible, so if Player 2 is known for Toxic Deluge rather than destroy effects, discount Flawless accordingly and this branch loses some shine.

And price the wrath correctly. The four tokens are gone forever, but Edgar dying once is survivable — eminence rebuilds a token per cast from the zone regardless — and Grave Pact and Cruel Celebrant sit in the 99 waiting to convert your next swept board into edicts and drains. The retaliatory wrath is partially monetized before it even resolves.

citations.quote: The window opens when your win attempt either can't be profitably answered — protection up, table tapped out, interaction counted and accounted for
If a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone.
A commander cast from the command zone costs an additional {2} for each previous time the player casting it has cast it from the command zone that game.
A token that’s in a zone other than the battlefield ceases to exist.

branches.choice: Keep Edgar zoned; cast Bloodline Keeper and Vampire Socialite
branches.line: Resolve the eminence token, then spend all six mana on two more Vampire spells: Bloodline Keeper ({2}{B}{B}) and Vampire Socialite ({B}{R}). Two casts bank two more eminence tokens. Attack with the six eligible bodies for six Sanctum drains — Player 3 to 6, not dead. Pass with a nine-plus-permanent board and Keeper ready to pump out 2/2 flyers.
branches.signals: This is the 'engine, not alpha' read — but the table sees a board that is now visibly one Edgar away from killing someone. To a competent Player 2 this does not read quieter than the alpha line. It reads like next turn's version of it, and it invites the wrath NOW, while your commander is uncast and your protection unpaid.
branches.coalition_risk: Medium this turn, maximal next. Nobody dies, so no one is forced to act — but a control player counting your board will not give you the untap. You also leave Player 3 alive at 6 to keep pressuring someone.
branches.coaching:
The trap in this line is the free-protection tension the strategic frame names: Flawless Maneuver costs a real {2}{W} while Edgar sits in the zone, and this line spends every mana. You are ten permanents deep into a telegraphed sweeper with no cover.

'Commit exactly as much as wins before it arrives, no further' is the operative rule, and this commitment does not win. Six drains leave everyone alive, so you take maximum wrath exposure for incremental value.

Eminence does soften the blow — the engine functions from the command zone by its own terms, so the rebuild is real. And yes, Grave Pact, Cruel Celebrant, and Viscera Seer live in the 99 to convert swept tokens into edicts, drains, and selection. But none of those pieces is on THIS board. The monetization is a deck fact, not a turn fact — you are trading a countable kill for a bigger board you may not keep.

This branch is right in one specific world: concrete evidence Player 2's four lands are bluff (they discarded at cleanup, or their known list runs sorcery-speed answers only). Absent that read, it is the greedy line wearing the patient line's clothes.

citations.quote: commit exactly as much as wins before it arrives, no further
An ability that states which zones it functions in functions only from those zones.

branches.choice: Commit small: Socialite only, hold real-mana protection
branches.line: Resolve the eminence token, cast only Vampire Socialite ({B}{R}), and attack with the six eligible bodies — six drains, Player 3 to 6. Hold four mana: enough to hard-cast Flawless Maneuver ({2}{W}) through the wrath, with a mana spare. Edgar waits for turn 7.
branches.signals: Passing with open mana from the deck that has cast a spell every turn reads as protection held — which is exactly true, and it may genuinely deter the wrath a turn. But the table also sees you NOT casting Edgar with six up. An observant player reads that as fear of the sweep you haven't drawn through.
branches.coalition_risk: Lowest of the three now, but every passive turn compounds toward Player 4 — the Simic engine drawing extra cards each turn is the seat that wins long games, and nobody at this table is pressuring them except you.
branches.coaching:
This is defensible wrath-math — wave one stays committed, the rebuild package stays in hand, protection is up. And patience is not a losing posture in this deck: with four verified pairings and three tutors in the 99, your inevitability against draw-go control is real.

But audit what the caution buys on THIS board. You hold Flawless for a board of tokens and lords you could rebuild anyway — eminence re-banks a token per cast, and Bloodline Keeper is still in hand as the post-wrath threat. The alpha line holds the SAME protection for free and kills a player with it.

And the seat that profits from your quiet turn is not the control deck. It is Player 4's Simic draw engine, which compounds regardless of whose inevitability is better on paper.

Take this line when the pivot genuinely isn't there. If Player 3 were at 20 instead of 12, no one dies through the alpha, and holding protection over a non-lethal swing becomes correct — the kill-web means the long game is yours to play. Here, with a countable elimination on the table, this is a turn of rent paid to fear.

citations.quote: don't overextend into an unknown sweeper without a reason

recommendation.choice: Cast Edgar now and alpha-strike with free Flawless Maneuver held
recommendation.rationale:
The three tests of the pivot window all pass. The win attempt is profitable even if answered — seven drains at declare attackers put 7 on every opponent and kill Player 3 before any wrath can intervene. The table's interaction is counted: Player 3 tapped out, Player 4 at two mana, Player 2's destroy-wrath covered by a {0} Flawless Maneuver that only exists because Edgar resolved. And failure leaves a rebuilt position: eminence functions from the command zone, every future Vampire cast re-banks a token, a died Edgar costs 8 next time, and the aristocrats layer means even a swept board pays you on the way out.

The goldfish makes the same argument from the other side. Edgar's median cast IS turn 6 (51.2% by t6, mean 6.628), and you hold protection in this window in 57.5% of games. The branches that keep him zoned either maximize wrath exposure with zero cover or pay a tempo tax to the one seat — the Simic engine — that profits from every quiet turn.

The kill-web buys you genuine lategame inevitability, but deferred inevitability never outbids a countable elimination with free protection held. Your threat level is structural; you cannot deflect your way out of it at six mana with a seven-attacker board. Take the label on the turn it kills a player.
